title: The Forester Who Invented Sustainable Forestry
event_summary: Hans Carl von Carlowitz, a mining administrator in Freiberg, Saxony, published 'Sylvicultura Oeconomica' in 1713 — the first comprehensive treatise arguing that forests must never be harvested faster than they regrow. Facing a devastating timber crisis that threatened to collapse Saxony's silver mining industry (which required enormous quantities of wood for smelting and tunnel supports), Carlowitz coined the term 'nachhaltende Nutzung' — sustained use — creating the foundational concept of sustainability. His book laid out systematic replanting schedules, species rotation, and long-term yield calculations that transformed forestry from reckless extraction into a managed science.
why_forgotten: Carlowitz died just one year after publication, and his dense German-language technical manual never reached a wide audience beyond Central European forestry circles. The concept of sustainability was later reinvented multiple times by economists and ecologists who rarely traced it back to an obscure Saxon mining bureaucrat. His work was also overshadowed by the more famous 18th-century French and British naturalists who received broader intellectual credit for environmental thinking.
why_it_matters: The word 'sustainability' — now the organizing principle of global climate policy, corporate governance (ESG), and the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals — descends directly from Carlowitz's 'Nachhaltigkeit.' German forestry science built on his model spread worldwide through colonial forestry programs in India, Southeast Asia, and Africa, shaping how every modern nation manages its natural resources. Without this single book by a mining official worried about running out of timber, the intellectual framework for confronting the climate crisis might have emerged decades later — or in a fundamentally different form.
